messages.subject: Re: point-level density/variance estimates
messages.body_plain:
Jennifer, it sounds to me like you might be better modelling the counts
as described in section 4.5 of the 2004 advanced distance sampling
book.  However, failing that, you will need to have a global detection
function model (your posting was unclear on this point), possibly using
the mcds engine if detectability may be a function of your habitat
covariates.  Of course, for any point with no detections, estimated
density will be zero, and the variance estimate will also be zero.
Bootstrapping won't help with that, and in any case, the main method of
bootstrapping in Distance is to resamples sampling units (points here),
which doesn't help you.  Generally for point data, there aren't
sufficient data to estimate density reliably by point, except by
developing a model for the counts, for example as in section 4.5 of the
2004 book.

Steve

messages.subject: Distance sampling workshops, August/September 2010,
messages.body_plain:
The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
(CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops in the summer of 2010 in our
purpose-built facilities at the University of St Andrews, Scotland. The
aim of these workshops is to train participants in the latest methods
for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys, including line and
point transects. The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the
field, using industry-standard software.

The first workshop (24-27 August) will run at an introductory level, and
will focus on "conventional" distance sampling methods, as described in
the standard reference book "Introduction to Distance Sampling." The
workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and participants will
learn how to use the program "Distance." Participants will gain a solid
grounding in both survey design and methods of analysis for distance
sampling surveys.

The advanced distance sampling workshop (30 August - 1 September) will
include advanced treatment of: incorporating covariates in detection
function modelling, analyses in which detectability on the transect line
is not assumed to be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem), automated
survey design, advanced stratified survey analysis, advanced trend
analysis, and adaptive survey designs. The aim of this workshop is to
bring participants up to date with the latest developments in distance
sampling methods and software. It is also an opportunity for those
actively engaged in the design, analysis and execution of distance
sampling surveys to discuss common issues and problems, and set future
research directions. The workshop will be a combination of lectures and
computer sessions, with considerable time for discussion.

For both workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data
sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.
Computer sessions take place in our modern computer classroom (attached
to the seminar room); participants can use our computers or bring their
own laptop computers.

Additional details regarding the workshop can be found at our website
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/distance2010/workshop_overview.html

messages.body_plain:
On 3/8/2010 3:48 PM, C. Blewett wrote:
> > hello and good afternoon list members,
> >
> > I have a problem with a completed survey where one distance interval having an extremely large number of observations compared those those on either side.  It's obviously heaping by observers.  (We'll be addressing this better in future surveys of course).
> >
> > The problem is that the interval has a really highly disproportionate number of observations.  Even grouping the numbers into a variety of intervals and seeing how that changes the results does not seem to help very much.  None of the models seem a really good fit, that one interval is affecting the detection curve.  Any solutions?  Would it be valid to delete a certain number of those observations?  Sort of like treating them as outliers?
Absolutely not.
> > Or perhaps truncating the data before that bin?
> >
> >
This is possible but if in fact the heaping is from observations at
distances less than the bin you'll create bias. You should decide on
bins that are based on the error in your distance measurements.
> > So one possibility I have found seems to be analyzing the data by season (rainy and dry), instead of pooling, as for one season this
> >   effect was much lower.  But I'd still like to check my logic on model-selection and goodness of fit.  Please give your opinions on the following points:
> >
> > Half-Normal with Cosine adjustment seemed to be the best fit model overall (to the rainy season data only), in my opinion.  The Hazard Rate with Cosine had a slightly smaller AIC (0.96 lower) but that's very slight. And the fit of the detection curve to the histogram appears visually worse with hazard rate, The curve starts above the histogram values at 0-10 (the first distance interval) than the half normal /
> > cosine, which started right at the top of the interval. The fit of the model closest to 0 is the most important correct?  So that's what I should be looking for?
> >
> > And furthermore, the density estimate (for Hazard rate) was a lot greater and I'd rather err to the side of lower density since those models AICs were so close anyway.  But the Chi-sq test had a better fit for the Hazard rate, but I don't think I want the curve to "fit" to a hump in the middle of the histogram, since it's not a real change in bird densities, it's observer heaping.  So how important should I rate that Chi-squared test between those 2 models?
Hard to know.  I think you are doing a little over-interpretation of the
fitting.  If the hazard model is grossly higher than the first bin that
may be a problem.  Have you done any right truncation?  It is quite
possible that you are simply out of luck if you can't trust your
distance measurements.  May want to focus a lot more effort on that.  As
much as we stress that in the book it is ignored time and again.
> >
> >
> > Half normal / Cosine ran with warnings "Constrained parameters to obtain monotonicity" but that's what I want it to do, I think!
In general yes. It is just letting you know that it is happening.
> > I do not want the detection curve to be increasing.  But the hazard rate model appears to vary more with the histogram intervals, but since there are heaped

messages.body_plain:
On 3/8/2010 9:40 PM, Philippe Bouchet wrote:
> > Dear list,
> >
> > Just another quick question regarding the interpretation of output graphs from MRDS
> > analyses, so as to make sure I am clear on this.
> >
> > In a survey with independent observers, the fitted functions on both observers' graphs of
> > detections (labelled Observer 1 detections&  Observer 2 detections) are above the
> > histogram bars at large distances, under the assumption of full independence. This means
> > that in spite of the inclusion of covariates in the model, unmodelled heterogeneity still
> > remains, doesn't it ? (and warrants the use of PI models) ?
> >
> >
Correct but the best measure is the AIC comparison between PI and FI
models,  I rarely see a real example in which PI is not favored over FI.
> > My other question relates to the interpretation of conditional detection plots, for the same
> > survey. I understand that these plots should be estimates of the detections functions for
> > both observers, however they might not be if observers only detect the most conspicuous
> > animals far away from the trackline. In my case, the proportion of duplicates increases
> > near the edge of my sampling strip, sometimes to reach a value of 1. Is it rightful to
> > state that this is indicative that observers were indeed only seeing the most detectable
> > animals ?
> >
Not certain of your question here.  The conditional detection plot is a
measure of what one observer sees from those seen by the other
observer.  If you select PI then that is exactly what it is but if you
use FI then you force that function to be equal to the detection for the
observer so it tries to fit both the distance data and the
marl-recapture data and usually fits both poorly.  First decide whether
that you should be using FI or PI and then look at the fit of the
detection functions relative to the data..

--jeff

messages.subject: Re: Snap shot point transects
messages.body_plain:
John, I'll send separately pdf's of the following papers:

Buckland, S.T. 2006.  Point transect surveys for songbirds:  robust
methodologies.  /The Auk/ *123*, 345-357.

Buckland, S.T., Marsden, S.J. and Green, R.E. 2008.  Estimating bird
abundance: making methods work.  /Bird Conservation International/ *18*,
S91-S108.

You will probably consider these to not be 'particularly in-depth'
though - that is essentially because there is not a lot to say about
it.  Conceptually, distance sampling is a snapshot method.  For species
where individuals move around very little, you can afford to stretch
this snapshot moment out over a longer time period.  For very mobile
species, you cannot.  The problem is that you want to ensure that
probability of detection at the point is certain (unless you use
mark-recapture methods), while at the same time recording positions of

snapshot moment only, but difficult to achieve, while ensuring that det
prob at the point is one.  In e.g. open, temperate woodland, for
breeding surveys of many songbird species at least, this is achievable.

messages.body_plain:
Adrian, it sounds like you need to examine your data and the fit of your=20
models.  You record observations by 50m bin, but it sounds like most of=20
your observations fall in the first bin, which will make them impossible=20
to model reliably.  Possibly adding in data for the rarer species has=20
made this problem worse.  This could happen for example if the rarer=20
species are less likely to be identified if they are beyond 50m, making=20
the apparent detection function very spiked.  g(0)=3D1 means exactly what=
=20
it suggests - det prob at distance zero is one.  It says nothing about=20
det prob in the interval 0-50m.

You need to look at why most of your data are in the first interval.  It=20
could be that your birds are not very detectable beyond the first 50m -=20
which suggests you have a poor choice of distance intervals.  However,=20
this seems unlikely for seabirds.  It may be that many of your birds are=20
in flight.  If you just record birds in flight at the position you first=20
detect them, this biases recorded distances towards zero - see the 2001=20
book (pp198-203) for discussion of this issue - and a suggested=20
solution.  It may be that many of your birds are being attracted towards=20
the vessel, and aren't being detected prior to this responsive=20
movement.  It may be that your observers are just estimating distances=20
visually without training - distances at sea are very difficult to=20
estimate, and it could be that birds well beyond 50m are being recorded=20
as if they're in the first interval.

The answer is likely to be in improving survey design and field=20
methods.  e.g. binocular search rather than naked eye search, aids to=20
estimating distances, training of fieldworkers for distance estimation=20
and species ID, revision of choice of distance intervals, revised=20
protocol for flying birds, etc.  You may not be able to extract anything=20
useful from existing data.  If you do continue with the analysis of=20
existing data, you can try truncating data beyond say 200m or 250m, to=20
see if that helps.  You will probably also need to over-ride the=20
automated model selection in Distance, and for example force Distance to=20
fit a half-normal detection function with no adjustments, to prevent it=20
fitting the spike in detections at zero distance.  However, you can=20
expect your density estimates to be biased, especially if the spike in=20
the first distance interval is real, rather than due to measurement=20
error or bird movement.

Steve Buckland

Below is what Tina sent me off-list.  The following is my advice. I'm
sending to the list as well in hopes that others might chime in. I think
this exchange demonstrates the importance of providing all of the
details about the study objective and design when you ask questions on
this list that request analysis advice rather than how-to questions
about DISTANCE.  The latter requires far less details than the former.

 From what I gather your main focus is to relate bird density to other
biological aspects and NOT to infer total abundance in a region. As
such, your primary focus is to estimate density on each transect in each
season. That's fine but it suggests a much different approach than
suggested by your initial query.  Given your description, I would create
12 strata (2 seasons * 6 transects) and within each strata I would
define a sample for each visit to that transect.  Then I would use MCDS
and I would investigate whether rainy/dry, transect, species and other
variables(?) might affect detection probability.  If you are
uncomfortable using transect, I'd at least consider using habitat or
some other variable that might differ by transect that could affect
detection probability.  If you reject this outright, you risk
confounding or adding noise to your analysis across transects with
detection variation.  You can fit additive models which require far
fewer parameters than fitting a separate detection function for each
species on each transect.

Then I'd estimate density by strata and if you want to bootstrap, you
can bootstrap samples within stratum which is using your replicate
visits to asses variation in density on each transect.  Personally, I
don't think you'll gain much from the bootstrap but you can certainly
try it.

Estimating average density across strata will be easy because if you
assign area=1 for each strata then you'll get the average density.
However, doing so within the rainy/dry season would be more difficult
but could be done by outside of Distance.  Alternatively, you could
split the analysis and do dry/rainy separately by selecting and
analyzing each set of strata separately.

The one gotcha in all of this is that your transect estimates will be
correlated unless you estimate detection separately for each species on
each transect.  That will complicate your later analysis and I suggest
that you may want to look at a recent paper that Steve Buckland wrote on
this subject.  Can't remember the citation at present but maybe Steve
can chime in.  regards --jeff

Hi Faye, List,

Despite some use (and most often abuse!) of distance sampling methods=20
from roads and other linear features with respect to which the animals=20
might respond, you have to remember a priori the following: conventional=20
distance sampling methods require that transects are laid at random with=20
respect to the animal distribution, therefore if the animals distribute=20
themselves non randomly with respect to the routes you'll have problems.=20
Note that even if the animals could not care less about the routes but=20
routes where positioned with respect to some body of water or shoreline,=20
and those are the only places where you always fin the animals, you'll=20
have problems too.

Given this, and regarding your specific questions below:

1. It really depends on whether you can assume that the distribution of=20
available geese is independent of the routes (in other words, and in the=20
case of line transects, if you could get the distance to all geese,=20
either detected or not, the methods should work if you saw an uniform=20
distribution and should fail if the distribution was far from uniform)

2. and 3. are related. You need to define a rule and stick to it.=20
Ideally it is easy to define what a cluster is. But if it is not easy to=20
do this, then you can create somewhat arbitrary rules and stick to those=20
(e.g. a cluster are all animals closer in space than 10 meters, or=20
sharing the same small body of water, or whatever - then you do need to=20
get the distance to the geometric center of the defined cluster).
4. you can, always trying to get the best distance possible. If they are=20
too far that a good range finder can not get their distance then likely=20
these distances will be truncated for the analysis any way.
5. there's no need to do it (but of course you get more data for the=20
detection function modeling if you do it twice, but not for the=20
encounter rate - you still have the same number of transects, just more=20
effort in each transect - often the way one would introduce that info=20
into distance, if you do not want inferences by each repeat, is to treat=20
each transect as being done just once with the double of the line length).

Hope this helps,

Tiago

messages.subject: Re: distance stats
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex, list,

Yes, I can easily make the change you ask.

The stats file is designed to be readily machine readable -- there are
no column headings, but its format is simple and is fully documented in
the online help (look in the index under "stats file", or in the MCDS
Engine Reference appendix).

I assume you're using some program to harvest the results you want from
the stats file.  Why not also use this program to run the analyses, and
thus bypass the graphic user interface altogether?  It's relatively
simple to program languages such as R to call the mcds analysis engine
(which is just an executable file) -- see previous postings to the list
about this, as well as the above cited appendix.

Alternatively, if this seems daunting, you might stick with the Distance
interface, but instead of getting the stats you need out of the stats
file, get them out of the Distnace project file (the .dst file, which is
just an Access 97 format database).  Some of the stats from the stats
file are saved there (for analyses that have been run), in the
AnalysisResultsStats table.  R (for example) has a package that can read
Microsoft Access tables, so it would be very easy to write code to
harvest the statistics you need, if they are saved.  In that table, ID
is the analysis ID, Parameter tells you what statistic it is, and value
is the value.

To find out which parameters are which, look in the Distance program
directory for DistIni.mdb.  In that, look in the ProjectSettings table.
  In that table, look for "Prm2" under the Section field.  The values in
the "Key" field are the parameter number, and the values under "Setting"
are their description (as they appear in the analysis browser).  They
appear again in the "PrmDesc" part of the Section field, with a longer
description under "value.  As an example, parameter 4020 is the
estimated density of individuals, and 4030 is estimated number of
individuals in the study area -- but only the global estimates are saved
(not the stratum-level ones).

Hope this is some help,

  - Len
